questions.question: What is the difference between type aliases and interfaces in TypeScript?
questions.title: Types Vs Interfaces
questions.direct_answer: Both define object shapes; the differences are mechanical. Interfaces: extend-able (extends), always object-shaped, support declaration merging (same name twice merges), better error messages for object literals. Type aliases: can name ANY type (unions, primitives, tuples, mapped types, conditional types), use intersection (&) for combination, and cannot merge — redeclaring is an error. Rule of thumb: interfaces for object/class contracts that others may extend; type for unions and type-level computation.

sections.title: Quick Revision
sections.content: Both define object shapes; the differences are mechanical. Interfaces: extend-able (extends), always object-shaped, support declaration merging (same name twice merges), better error messages for object literals. Type aliases: can name ANY type (unions, primitives, tuples, mapped types, conditional types), use intersection (&) for combination, and cannot merge — redeclaring is an error. Rule of thumb: interfaces for object/class contracts that others may extend; type for unions and type-level computation.

sections.title: Interview Answer
sections.content:
The split, verified conceptually:

```ts
// INTERFACE — object contracts, open for extension
interface User { name: string; }
interface Admin extends User { permissions: string[]; }   // extends ✓

// Declaration merging — same name merges (module augmentation's basis)
interface Window { myGlobal: string; }   // adds to the built-in Window

// TYPE — names ANY type
type ID = string | number;               // union — interfaces CAN'T do this
type Pair = [string, number];              // tuple
type Named = { name: string };
type Admin2 = Named & { permissions: string[] };  // intersection combines
```

The capability matrix (the interview core):

```
                      interface    type
object shapes         ✓            ✓
extends/combines      extends      & intersection
unions/tuples         ✗            ✓
mapped/conditional    ✗            ✓
declaration merging   ✓            ✗ (redeclare = error)
implements (classes)  ✓            ✓ (object-shaped ones)
error messages        clearer      can alias to confusing names
```

The practical guidance (the answer that shows judgment): for public object contracts and anything consumers should extend — interface (merging lets library users augment). For unions, computed types, function signatures as building blocks — type. Teams that standardize on one are fine; the real rule is consistency and knowing the trade-offs.

The subtlety worth naming: interfaces are 'open' — declaring `interface X {}` twice merges the members, which enables module augmentation (adding fields to third-party types). Type aliases are 'closed' — two declarations of the same name are a compile error. This openness is a feature (extensibility) and a hazard (accidental merge across files with the same name).

sections.title: Mental Model
sections.content:
```mermaid
flowchart TD
    subgraph interface
        I[object contracts] --> E[extends - chains]
        I --> M[declaration merging - open]
    end
    subgraph type
        T[any type] --> U[unions / tuples]
        T --> A[intersection and-combines]
        T --> C[mapped / conditional types]
    end
```

sections.title: Deep Dive
sections.content:
The extension mechanics differ (the internals): interface extends and type intersection (&) both combine object shapes, but nominal behaviors diverge on conflicting members — interface extension ERRORS on incompatible re-declared properties, while & silently creates a type where the conflicting property is never — a property typed never is unusable, and the error surfaces only where it's used, far from the declaration. This is why intersection-conflicts are a classic TS debugging question.

The performance angle (the compiler's reality): interfaces historically created better type-display caches — in huge codebases, type aliases of object literals can produce slower compilation and worse error output (the alias name shows, not the expanded shape). The TS team has narrowed this gap; the remaining practical difference is error readability for object literals: 'Type X is missing properties' beats a giant anonymous union expansion.

The modern convergence (the closing note): since TS 4.x, the official style guidance (and the TS handbook) says: choose interfaces first for object shapes, use types when you need features interfaces lack — unions, intersections of non-objects, mapped types, conditional types, template literal types. The differences that once forced the choice (implements, extends, merging) now work on both sides for the common cases; the remaining hard boundary is: unions and type-level computation are type-alias-only territory.
